{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. @ajs, dev_reflow2 hub session, 2026-09-27: "I was going to say we could put the reflow2 there also, but I'm concerned that we don't have all the tools. then again, if I keep this dev_reflow2 at running locally, it would still have all 193 tools."

TODAY: reflow2's design is a local store beside its repository, reached by the hub's child-reflow2 connection with all 193 tools. The combined plan moves it last among the moves (position 11, after flo2's), as dec:idea-a-repo-that-holds-its-design-moves-it-to-a-remote-server-once set.

WHAT THE CONCERN TURNS ON, measured the same night:
- The tools actually missing through api.flo2.io are fewer than 17. Of the 17 flo2 refuses, seven take their evidence from the caller and read nothing on the host (flo2's fact:only-wall-check-of-the-machine-side-tools-reads-files-itself-2026-09-27); flo2 schedules five of them at combined position 2, and the other two are the same kind. What genuinely stays missing is wall_check (it reads the files itself), the seven that read other designs by path (combined position 12), and two that stay off by design.
- ⚠️ "KEEP dev_reflow2 LOCAL WITH ALL 193" ONLY HOLDS FOR DESIGNS WHOSE STORE IS ON THIS MACHINE. The hub reaches each child through that child's own server. A design moved to flo2.io is reached through flo2.io's gateway, and reflow2's local client (`--remote`) forwards to that same gateway, so it gets the same 176 today. A local server cannot serve the full list for a design it does not hold.
- reflow2's own work leans harder on the missing and not-yet-remote pieces than flo2's does: CI runs wall_check against the design, release cuts freeze checksums measured on the build machine (position 10), and the export-based CI gate (position 9).
- 🛑 BOOTSTRAP, SHARPER THAN FOR flo2: flo2.io's engine IS reflow2. An engine release that breaks opening designs would also make reflow2's design, the one you would read to fix it, unreachable from flo2.io.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN:
(a) Keep reflow2's design local for good; flo2.io hosts everyone else's. Cheapest; gives up "one blueprint on a server" for the engine's own design.
(b) Move it where the plan has it (11), once CI, release cuts and wall_check have a remote route.
(c) Move it early and accept the gaps. The largest cost of the three: reflow2's CI and release process depend on exactly what is missing.

═══ 2026-09-30 — @AJS BRAINSTORMS THE MOVE AGAIN. RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING; nothing chosen. ═══
In his words: "I really want to figure out how to push reflow2 to flo2.io, but I believe there is some issues with how changelog.md is updated and how the design is tracked in the reflow2 github repo. If the design is held in flo2.io for reflow2, could just before a PR, could we export the design, download it locally and then update the change log accordingly and then merge? The design is then always up to speed with that last PR. We could also remove the design completely from the reflow2 design and then only have to worry about how to figure out how to update the change log?"

HIS TWO SHAPES, mapped onto what is already settled:
(c1) MOVE NOW AND COMMIT A COPY PER PR, which is option (c) with flo2's bridge. Before merge, take the copy from flo2.io and commit it as the PR's last commit; CI reads it. This is exactly how flo2 works today (flo2 cap:flo2s-design-is-hosted-and-ci-reads-a-copy; used today by flo2 #110).
(c2) MOVE AND KEEP NO DESIGN IN THE REPO. This is the settled END STATE: combined position 11 retires the copy, under dec:idea-one-blueprint-the-store-is-the-design-and-an-export-is-a-perishable-photocopy. It is planned AFTER position 9 (epoch:planned-ci-asks-the-blueprint), because without it CI has no design to check the code against.

THE PAIN HE NAMES IS REAL, and measured in this repo:
- every parallel PR carries an export, so the design file conflicts, needs the merge driver, and once showed a ~115-line change as a ~380,000-line rewrite (fact:the-merge-driver-writes-the-merged-export-in-a-different-byte-layout-than-the-exporter-2026-09-22);
- #620's CI failed when its export grew;
- branch records need worktree-private stores, and live records need folding back (#637);
- the live store sits on whatever branch the checkout is on: 2026-09-30, 19 commits behind main, and a status read from it was wrong;
- CHANGELOG's Unreleased section conflicts on every parallel PR. That half is recorded separately on dec:idea-how-changelog-md-gets-written-once-the-design-is-the-record.

FOR (c1):
- It removes the three-way design merge. The server is the one truth, so at merge time the PR simply re-copies the latest; there is nothing to reconcile.
- It keeps reflow2's design PUBLIC: the repo copy is public, and flo2.io designs are private, with "make a design public" planned, not built.
- The newest copy in git is the bootstrap fallback this node's 🛑 asks for: a broken engine release can be recovered from it by local import.

AGAINST (c1), kept beside it:
- The blocker was never the copy. reflow2's own loop leans on what api.flo2.io does not yet serve: wall_check, local-file measurement against a remote design (position 7), the eight path-reading tools (position 12), and release-cut checksums on the build machine (position 10).
- With one hosted design, a branch's design writes land in the SHARED design before merge. Parallel branches see each other's in-flight records, and an abandoned PR leaves records for code that never merged. Today's worktree-private stores exist to prevent exactly that. It is open question (c) of the photocopy decision, unanswered.
- flo2's copy script has a measured gap: ops/flo2-design-copy cannot pass accept_divergence, so a deliberate edge removal blocked it on 2026-09-30.

SIZE: (c1) is medium. Copy plus CI already exist for flo2. The cost is the per-branch-records question and working without the unserved tools.
(c2) is large and ordered. It needs position 9: CI reaching flo2.io means a credential in a PUBLIC repo's CI, and fork PRs cannot read secrets. #616 came from an outside team. It also loses public readability until public designs exist.

═══ 2026-09-30, LATER — @AJS ASKS FOR "IDEAS TO COUNTERACT" THE TWO OBJECTIONS TO (c1). Recorded as brainstorming; nothing chosen. ═══

OBJECTION 2 (branch records in one hosted design) already has a designed answer, waiting for his word: dec:how-a-branchs-implementation-facts-are-held. Its option (a) is a per-branch overlay; option (d), added today, is design changes replayed from the PR at merge. The hosted-specific consequences are noted there.

OBJECTION 1 (the tools api.flo2.io does not serve) is mostly answered by accepted intent and planned steps:
- req:the-local-client-opens-the-persons-files-for-the-tools-that-name-one (accepted): wall_check and the seven path-reading tools run through the person's own client, which opens the files locally;
- combined position 7: local files are measured for a remote design;
- combined position 10: a release cut against a remote design;
- combined position 12: the file-opening tools.
Today's options here are about ORDER and INTERIM, not about whether:
(i) PULL 7, 10 AND 12 FORWARD as the move's critical path, ahead of positions they do not depend on.
(ii) MOVE THE FRONT DOOR, NOT THE STORE. flo2.io routes callers to a reflow2 design whose home stays on the machine that holds the repository, where every tool works (flo2's req:any-node-serves-a-caller-to-the-design-wherever-it-lives, proposed; its capability planned). People reach reflow2's design through flo2.io, while its store and files stay together.
  - AGAINST: the design is reachable only while that machine is up, and exposing a home machine to flo2's gateway is a new attack surface. It also does not retire the local server.
(iii) CI AS THE FILE-MEASURING CLIENT. CI holds the checkout. It runs the local client against the hosted design and sends checksums as asserted, which covers positions 7 and 9 for the gate.
  - AGAINST: CI then needs a flo2.io credential, which a public repo's fork PRs cannot read.

SIZES: (i) is the plan's own work, re-ordered. (ii) is medium-large on flo2's side, plus an operational risk.
